title: Reward Pathway and Tolerance
description: Schematic p5.js simulation of the brain's dopamine reward pathway (VTA to nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex). Natural rewards produce a moderate dopamine bump and drug doses a large spike; repeated doses downregulate receptors, shrinking responses and lowering the baseline (tolerance), and stopping the drug produces a below-baseline dip (withdrawal) that recovers over simulated days.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
learningObjectives: Explain how repeated drug doses produce tolerance: smaller dopamine responses and a lower baseline caused by receptor downregulation.
Explain why stopping a drug after tolerance produces a below-baseline withdrawal state that recovers slowly as receptors return.
Compare the size and speed of the dopamine response to a natural reward with the response to an addictive drug.
prerequisites: Basic brain regions: midbrain and prefrontal cortex (Chapter 4)
keyQuestions: Why does each repeated drug dose produce a smaller dopamine spike?
Why do natural rewards feel less rewarding after tolerance develops?
Why does stopping the drug make signaling drop below even the lowered baseline?
How long does recovery take in the model, and what does the model leave out?
misconceptions: Dopamine is simply a 'pleasure chemical' (it also signals surprise, importance, and motivation).
Each dose of a drug feels the same no matter how often it is used.
Stopping a drug immediately returns the brain to normal.
Addiction is only a matter of willpower and involves no brain changes.
dataNote: All values are illustrative relative units in a schematic model; they are not measurements of any real drug.
